en: Your father passed from this world,
The youngest of six lions,
God's beloved mortal.
All fortune was complete in him.
If you looked within him,
He was broader than the earth.
No one caused him harm;
None remained to raise a herding pole against him.
Your distinguished leopard of a father,
Hardened by drinking much blood,
Was also named the conquering lord.
For the iron city of Mecca,
Your father was a fortress.
For the Muslims, a mere handful,
An iron city for these people
Was what your father had become.
The unbelievers' herds, he shattered
And scattered—such was your father.
The Muslims' road, wide open,
Was opened by your father.
Into vast, looming Beijing,
When he drove straight in and thrust his spear,
From hell's grievous torment,
When he freed his soul,
Because of Judgment Day,
Because of the hair-thin bridge,
The forty Chinese tribes of Kakanchi,
When they shouted and thrust their spears,
The forty Chinese tribes of Kakanchi,
When they fought without looking back,
All the lions favored by Khizyr died.
When they were hard pressed,
Twelve pairs of khans went,
Four hundred and twenty thousand troops went.
Many souls of diverse kinds came.
Aykhojo of Mecca,
For the handful of Muslims,
Came to minister to their faith.
Banner-bearing Khan Koshoy
Came from the Katagan.
Mighty Bakay, who knew the unknown,
The world's rival;
Ajybay, son of Argyn Khan,
Of the eighteen thousand worlds
Was the interpreter who passed between them.
Almambet, son of Azozyl,
Was the lion of all the world's peoples.
Chubak, son of Akbaltay,
Was the world's champion.
Syrgak, son of Ulak Khan,
Was Manas's close companion.
His strength reached across the world.
He and Manas, those two,
Were sons of brothers.
Never resting upon an elbow,
Never taking a wink of sleep,
The finest of the sixty,
The strongest of the forty companions—
In the bloody slaughter, the burning embers,
In the great campaign to Kakan,
Seek them, my son: none remains alive.
That great slaughter at Kakan
Was begun by your leopard of a father.
This world that stands here,
Your father, too, left it thus.
When he campaigned against Beijing,
Leading an elephant and firing shots,
I went along with him.
Your fierce father—
My foal, I witnessed his lion's courage.
Besieging Beijing,
He took a thousand of its khans.
Of the stone-worshipping Chinese,
The finest were captured.
Thimble-mouthed and camel-calf-eyed,
Of the gracefully swaying beauties,
A hundred and twenty thousand were driven away.
Cursed be their capture!
Many a delightful lion died;
Egizey and Koshoy both died.
The giants Almambet and Chubak died;
All who met Beijing died.
Heroes died upon the road they scouted;
Struck with a spear from the flank,
Your mighty father Manas
Returned wounded to Talas,
Passed to the other world, and died as well.
No one spoke harm against him.
From your father, Sultan Manas,
No one who faced him returned.
When all the warriors had died,
When the Muslim people suffered torment,
When Akkula was shot down,
And your father suffered hardship on foot,
At Acha-Tash's broad pass,
When your father was left on foot,
The skilled horseman and swift runner,
The treasury's great marksman,
One learned in marvels,
Whose very fame struck fear,
When he was driving them toward Mecca,
Your father first among the giants,
When he was about to bind them all,
Your father, who has gone to Judgment,
Began the slaughter from the slope.
Kozhozhash foremost among them,
Eight Chinese champions,
Your father, Khan Manas,
Killed them all with a single shot.
He broke the unbelievers' strength,
And calmed the Muslims' hearts.
Such a lion was your father.
While you were still a babe in the cradle,
Orphan, you were the one he left behind.
Breaking palaces and taking booty,
Stirring strife on right and left,
When he raided and shattered the Afghans,
Akylay, daughter of Shooruk,
Was the wife he seized by force.
When he brought havoc to Bukhara,
When he plundered its possessions,
Scattering livestock, giving herds,
Saying, 'Surely she will prove excellent,'
Your mother Kanykei,
For countless livestock paid as bride-price,
Was the wife he chose and took.
He took the two together.
Keeping forty companions, making them lions,
Making them his own near equals,
Touched by Khizyr, stirred to frenzy,
With all the mighty men assembled,
While he maintained his wealth,
He sent his forty companions forth,
And scouted the face of the earth.
Your father, Khan Manas,
Taking two wives at once,
The poor man still had no offspring.
In the autumn before he went on campaign,
On the plain of Karkyra,
At Kara-Saz in Karkyra,
When the mares were tethered,
When friendship was made with the kaldai,
And salt was boiled,
At Khan Kökötöy's funeral feast,
Before that great assembly,
The Muslim and infidel champions—
I saw them file past.
Ezkara, khan of the Manchus,
Was a fellow of formidable judgment;
All those infidels and Muslims—
I saw him assess them.
Shouting the battle cry “Khan Manas!”
The countless Chinese and many Manchus—
I saw them weep that day.
'Ah, Manas is a true hero!
Throughout the whole wide world this Burut
Stands alone, a lion.
He wears a black fur cap like a cauldron;
The world's four corners
He has the power to slaughter single-handed.
Against a man like this,
What person could hold his own?
Against a khan like this—
Even to Kakan Khan's Beijing
This lion's word would carry.
To the handful of Muslims,
He would lend his strength, this hero.'
To see if he was a hero,
To learn the measure of his honor,
To put his strength to trial,
Those countless Chinese and Manchus
Could not refrain from stirring trouble.
Among the Muslim champions,
'Which one is the strongest?' they asked,
And could not leave them untested.
Refusing the meat and making a quarrel,
The infidels' Ezkara,
From Khan Koshoy himself,
From all four corners of the world,
Maaniker could bring news;
He demanded Maaniker:
'Obey what I say, Burut,
Give me Maaniker, Burut!
If you will not obey,
If you will not give me Maaniker,
I will have no this or that;
I will not eat the meat you serve.
I will not bend and camp beside you;
I will never make peace with you.
Obey me now, Burut,
Give me Maaniker, Burut!
This Maaniker standing here—
Its broad crupper flaring,
He is a mount for a kaldai to ride,
With his battle apron tied about him,
A mount to ride to Beijing.
Among the jewel-wearing Chinese,
He is a horse for the purest to ride.
Among the black Kalmyks in sleeveless coats,
He is a mount for the mightiest.
To bear loads of gold and silver,
To present to Esen Khan,
Maaniker is a fitting courser.
To ride at feasts and celebrations,
To make him prance about,
He has just the right disposition.
I will turn to no other horse;
I will not rest without Maaniker.
If you will not obey my words,
If you will not give me Maaniker,
Name the support you rely upon;
Name the place where you will fight hard.
Name your steep and lofty pass;
I will not spare my thread of life against you—
Name the place for our slaughter!
Obey what I say, Burut,
Catch him and give him to me now, Burut!'
The infidels' Ezkara,
With countless wrestlers at his side,
Made him yellow as with jaundice,
Pressing him without end.
Bokmurun, twelve years old,
Those darting words of his
He heard at that moment.
Hearing them, he writhed;
Bokmurun, Kökötöy's son,
Wept before the multitude.
'I will plait each hair of your tail,
My inheritance from my father,
My beloved Maaniker—
How can I give you to this Chinese?'
With his girdle hung about his neck,
At his wits' end, his strength fled;
The red blood drained from his face.
Speaking through tears, in anguish,
Bokmurun, Kökötöy's son,
Pleaded with the hero Koshoy:
'Of paradise lying idle,
You opened the door, my heroic uncle;
Of the bazaar held bound,
You unlocked its fortune, my heroic uncle!
While my father, great Kökötöy, lived,
Uncle Koshoy, listen—
I went too far in my intoxication.
Among infidels and Muslims,
Scattering livestock,
My dear khan and uncle,
I did harm to my own life.
A playful child, in my pampered days,
I dreamed of a yearling ewe's congealed fat.
Koshoy, great as a mountain, hear me:
Today I have seen hell's immensity.
Uncle Koshoy, listen now:
I was pampered in my childhood;
I lost my father, Khan Kökötöy,
And this year I am twelve.
